sections.title: Problems with Traditional Fundraising
sections.content:
Traditional crowdfunding platforms like GoFundMe, Kickstarter, and Indiegogo have helped millions of people raise money for their projects and causes. But they come with strings attached that most people do not think about until it is too late. These platforms act as gatekeepers. They decide which campaigns are allowed to exist, they can freeze funds at any time, and they take a significant cut of every dollar raised. GoFundMe charges around 2.9% plus 30 cents per donation in payment processing fees. Kickstarter takes 5% of successfully funded projects on top of payment processing fees. For a campaign that raises $50,000, that is thousands of dollars that never reach the creator.

The gatekeeper problem goes deeper than fees. In 2022, GoFundMe froze millions of dollars raised for the Canadian Freedom Convoy, citing terms of service violations. Regardless of your opinion on the convoy itself, the precedent is alarming. A private company decided that millions of willing donors could not send their money to a legal cause. This has happened repeatedly around the world. During the Nigerian EndSARS protests in 2020, the government pressured payment platforms to freeze accounts of protest organizers. Donations through traditional channels were blocked overnight. The message is clear: if your cause is unpopular with the powerful, your funding can disappear with a phone call.

There is also the problem of access. Traditional crowdfunding platforms require bank accounts, government identification, and often restrict participation to certain countries. A brilliant inventor in Lagos, a social entrepreneur in Caracas, or an artist in Nairobi may have ideas worth funding but lack the banking infrastructure to use platforms designed for people in New York and London. The global crowdfunding market is worth over $17 billion, but the vast majority of that money flows within wealthy countries, leaving the rest of the world largely excluded from participation.

sections.title: Bitcoin-Native Crowdfunding
sections.content:
Bitcoin-native crowdfunding platforms strip away the gatekeepers and connect creators directly with supporters anywhere in the world. Platforms like Geyser Fund operate entirely on Bitcoin and the Lightning Network, meaning anyone with a Bitcoin wallet can create a campaign or make a donation. There is no bank account requirement, no government ID check, and no corporate committee deciding whether your project deserves to exist. If people want to fund your idea, they can, and nobody in the middle can stop them.

Geyser Fund has already funded hundreds of projects across dozens of countries. Bitcoin education programs in Africa, open-source software tools, independent journalism operations, community mesh networks, and creative projects of every kind have found funding through the platform. Because it uses the Lightning Network, a supporter in Tokyo can fund a project in Nairobi in under one second, with fees measured in fractions of a cent. Try sending $10 from Japan to Kenya through PayPal and see how much actually arrives. The friction of traditional cross-border payments has been a massive barrier to global crowdfunding, and Lightning removes it almost entirely.

The transparency of Bitcoin adds another dimension. Every donation is recorded on a public ledger, so supporters can verify that funds were received. Some platforms are building tools that let donors track how funds are spent, creating a level of accountability that traditional crowdfunding has never offered. There is no corporate intermediary holding the money in escrow, deciding when to release it, or threatening to return it to donors if arbitrary conditions are not met. The money flows directly from supporter to creator, settled in minutes rather than weeks.

sections.title: Lightning Tips and Value-for-Value
sections.content:
The value-for-value model is a concept that Bitcoin and the Lightning Network have made practical for the first time. The idea is simple: instead of paying a subscription fee upfront or watching advertisements, you consume content freely and then pay whatever you think it was worth. If a podcast episode changed your life, you send 10,000 satoshis. If it was just okay, you send 100. If it was not for you, you send nothing. The creator gets paid based on the actual value they provide, and the audience decides what that value is.

This model is already thriving. Podcasting apps like Fountain and Breez let listeners stream satoshis to podcast hosts in real time as they listen. The payments happen automatically, second by second, through Lightning. Writers on platforms like Stacker News earn Bitcoin for articles and comments that the community finds valuable. Musicians are embedding Lightning tip jars on their websites and social media profiles, letting fans support them directly without a label or streaming platform taking the majority of the revenue. These are not theoretical experiments. Real creators are earning real money this way, every single day.

The implications for crowdfunding are significant. Instead of running a single campaign and hoping to hit a funding goal, creators can build ongoing relationships with their supporters through continuous value-for-value exchanges. A documentary filmmaker does not need to raise all the money upfront. They can release episodes as they go, earning Lightning tips from viewers who appreciate the work. An open-source developer does not need corporate sponsors. They can receive tips from the users who benefit from their code. This is a fundamentally different funding model, one where the relationship between creator and supporter is direct, ongoing, and based on genuine value rather than marketing hype.
